stories.title: Spanish PM calls early election amid housing protests
stories.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called an early election for 29 November, in a bid to strengthen his mandate after a fragmented parliament rejected the government's key housing decrees last week amid widespread protests. "We need to renew people's support," Mr Sanchez said in a televised address. "We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain." The prime minister also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises. "I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today," he said. The defeat in parliament on Friday was another political setback for the Socialist prime minister, which renewed questions over whether his minority government could have survived until the next scheduled general election in 2027.

stories.title: Blood Transfusion Service issues urgent donor appeal
stories.summary: The Irish Blood Transfusion Service has issued an urgent appeal for people with RhD negative blood to donate. Stocks are running particularly low for O negative blood, with supplies expected to fall below three days by tomorrow. The Director of Donor Experience and Collections with the Irish Blood Transfusion Service has said the shortage of negative blood types is due to a drop-off in donations and an increase in the use of blood for surgeries. Ms Ryan said only 3% of the eligible population donate blood, yet one in four of us will need donated blood at some point throughout our lifetime. "This particular blood type can be under pressure because 8% of the population is O negative, yet it accounts for 16% of all of the blood that we issue. It’s the universal blood type. "It's used in stem cell transplant emergencies. It's used for very small babies and for some blood disorders and that creates that supply and demand tension."

stories.title: Services sector expands, new business hits 10-month high
stories.summary: The country's services sector expanded in September as demand strengthened and new business grew at its fastest pace in 10 months, a business survey showed today. The AIB Ireland Services Business Activity Index, compiled by S&P Global, fell to 54.1 from 55.4 in August, a survey by S&P Global showed. New business rose for a fifth month in a row and at the strongest rate since November 2025. Export business also increased for a fifth month, but only marginally, with Business Services the only sector to record a decline. Capacity pressures intensified as outstanding work increased for a fourth consecutive month, and at the fastest pace since August 2024. Employment returned to growth after August's pause, although the pace of hiring was described as relatively weak. Cost pressures strengthened, with input price inflation accelerating to its highest since May, driven by wages and higher fuel and energy costs.

stories.title: Bačka Topola: an unusual venue for an Irish 'home' game
stories.summary: Bačka Topola, a one hour and 40-minute drive north of the Serbian capital, Belgrade, is an unlikely place to host a competitive international match, especially one as contested as tonight's second Republic of Ireland versus Israel fixture. The car journey to the small town of about 12,000 inhabitants cuts through flat landscape dotted with small villages. Not particularly known for its footballing prowess, Bačka Topola is better known in Serbia for a nearby stud farm and a picturesque lake. But the town also has an impressive, albeit small stadium, the TSC Arena with a capacity of 4,500 seats. The home of Serbian second division outfit FK TSC, the stadium has also hosted Israeli club Maccabi Tel Aviv's European 'home' matches in recent years. That could explain why the FAI opted for this remote town as the venue for tonight's fixture behind closed doors.

stories.title: McMillan: CEO search will be no distraction for Munster
stories.summary: Munster head coach Clayton McMillan doesn't believe the province’s search for a new chief executive will be a distraction from his day-to-day business, as the hunt for Ian Flanagan’s replacement begins. Flanagan confirmed on Thursday that he would step down as CEO at the end of October, following a year of turbulence off the pitch last season. Munster’s players certainly looked unaffected by the off-field change on Saturday night, as 20-year-old out-half Charlie O’Shea starred in a 26-22 bonus-point win against the Bulls, which saw the province pick up their first win of the URC season. After the game, McMillan was asked if the changes at the top of the organisation could be a distraction for his playing group, and the New Zealander gave a typically blunt response. "If we compare it to last year, this is a walk in the park," he replied. "I'm not trying to say that the decision isn’t a big one that Ian's made, but again, he's made that decision and we respect it and we wish him and his family all the best.

stories.title: Fitzmaurice: Quality of players drew me to Galway job
stories.summary: New Galway senior football manager Éamonn Fitzmaurice says the quality of the squad was the over-riding reason he stepped back into senior inter-county management after an eight-year absence. He has also stayed coaching at club level – bringing Fossa to the All-Ireland junior title in 2023 and also leading his home club Finuge to the Kerry JFC. Over the past number of years his name was regularly linked to several vacancies, but nothing ever materialised. Fitzmaurice works as principal of Pobalscoil Chorcha Dhuibhne in Dingle, and has a young family, thus inter-county management was not believed to be a priority. "Paul Bellew (chairman) reached out the weekend after Pádraic stepped down," he said. "I’ve had these calls over the last couple years, but it has never gone beyond a phone call. My head was turned this time, and I said maybe, out of curiosity, I’d explore it.

stories.title: Press briefing ends abruptly as FAI reject racism claims
stories.summary: The end of what has been at times a trying week for Irish football draws near. Ireland play their 'home' game against Israel in Serbia on Sunday evening, thus concluding this block of four games in the Nations League. As things stand, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side have four points from three games. Asked whether a return of seven from their last three encounters would be a satisfactory return, the Irish boss took a broader view, when speaking at a press conference ahead of the game. A gathering that ended rather abruptly after a disagreement between an Israeli journalist and FAI communications officer Kieran Crowley, with the journalist claiming that Irish players had called Israeli players "monkeys". Crowley responded by saying: "that's completely untrue" and declaring that the press conference was finished. A briefing for Irish media only then took place in a separate room but a member of the Israeli broadcast media tried to join in. This led to the briefing being moved to another section of the stadium. "Surviving this camp, coming out of it together as one would be a massive win for me," Hallgrimsson had said earlier.

stories.title: Bond & Buckley to Baldur's Gate: Irish actors making it in gaming
stories.summary: Whether it's TV, film or theatre, on stage or on screen, the Irish have always punched above their weight, delivering mesmerising performances that continue to set the standard in the entertainment industry. We are a nation of storytellers, after all. And in the world of gaming, that’s still the case. Several Irish actors have become central to some of the best games you can play, captivating us as endearing characters and helping sculpt stories we still think fondly of today. From action and adventure to psychological horror, comedy and more, here’s a quick rundown of some of the best appearances from the Irish you can find on a console. While the film industry drags its heels in deciding who will take on the 007 mantle, Irishman Patrick Gibson is leading the charge on the gaming front, portraying Bond in the brand-new 007 First Light, released earlier this year. The game is an original take on the early parts of Bond's career, and became a critical success upon release, with Gibson’s performance receiving its due acclaim. The actor brings the inexperience of a fledgling agent to the forefront, while still developing his suave, signature silver tongue. With the Game of the Year awards only a few short months away, expect Gibson to be in contention in the performance category. And hopefully, he’ll carry on the mantle of the digital Bond well into the future.

stories.title: Ireland to send two youngsters to Junior Eurovision
stories.summary:
Teenagers Caleb Kirwan and Naomi Gribben have been chosen to represent Ireland at this month's Junior Eurovision Song Contest in Malta. In the Irish Junior Eurovision Final on TG4 on Sunday, the judges were unable to choose between the singers and decided both should go to Malta. Caleb, 14, from Dublin, and Naomi, 13, from Co Down, will represent Ireland with the song Níos Láidre (Stronger) on Saturday, 24 October. Of the two young singers, TG4 says: "From a very young age, Caleb has loved performing and finds immense joy in singing, dancing, and acting. A natural entertainer, he thrives on stage and loves connecting with audiences through performance. The stage is where Caleb feels most at home; it is his happy place where he can truly express himself.

"Caleb has been training in singing, dancing, and acting since the age of six and currently studies at Steptacular Performing Arts School in Dublin. Over the years, he has performed a wide range of principal roles, most recently portraying Lumière in Beauty and the Beast, Buttons in Cinderella, Peter in Mary Poppins, and Jamie in Everybody's Talking About Jamie. He is also part of the Elite dance team and recently performed in the Dance World Cup, coming fourth overall in the boys' hip-hop category.

"Naomi gets her singing talents from her nanny and grandad, a gift she shares with all her cousins. When she's not singing, Naomi loves ice skating with her friends, acting, and shopping, but only if she can spend her mum's money.

"Naomi is no stranger to the stage, and it's where she feels most at home. In fact, in 2025, she was the only singer from Ireland and the UK to make it to the finals of the Tour Music Fest in San Marino. She hopes that there will be more stages for her to sing on in the future. But her main passion is using her singing ability to help others. Last year she busked in her local town, and she gave all the money to support local people living with cancer." The Junior Eurovision Song Contest Final will take place on Saturday, 24 October in Ta' Qali, Attard, Malta, and will be shown on TG4 from 8pm.

stories.title: The 2 Johnnies on friendship, fatherhood, and 10 years of showbiz
stories.summary: As The 2 Johnnies return with season four of their Late Night Lock In, Janice Butler talks to Johnny Smacks and Johnny B about staying true to themselves after 10 years in showbiz, those Up for the Match rumours, and Smacks becoming a dad. Rarely seen apart, when our Zoom starts, I get a surprise when Johnny Smacks is sitting in a room on his own. "The other lad is signing on now in a minute. We’re in separate locations for once," he laughs. "You’re one of the lucky ones to see us separately. We’re about 5km from each other; I’m at home combining babysitting and a few house bits, and he’s in the studio," he adds, referring to his baby boy JJ who arrived 10 months ago. Within minutes, Johnny B bursts onto the screen. "Hello, hello, hello," he calls down the camera. "I like your fridge," he says, commenting on all the magnets and kids’ art on the fridge behind me. "I’m the same with fridge magnets, from pubs Johnny and I have been to and kicked out of; more of them from the ones we’ve been kicked out of," he laughs. They’re in fine form, and why wouldn’t they be? This Christmas, they’ll celebrate 10 years of their 2 Johnnies podcast, that is rarely out of the top three in the charts, and they have a sold-out 3Arena show to top off another big year for the pair from Cahir. The summer saw them welcome 20,000 fans to their Pints in a Field show in Dublin; then Johnny B went to the States on his holidays and Smacks "stayed in the back yard" with his wife Annie and new son JJ, who finally made it home to Tipperary in February after four months in Crumlin, following a diagnosis of gastroschisis and five surgeries after his birth. "It was a busy summer," says Smacks. "We had Pints in a Field, and then after that you have a sweet spot where you get a couple of weeks to chill and then it’s straight back to planning the TV show and the Christmas show. You never get too long to rest on your laurels. Johnny went to America on his holidays and I went to the back yard," he laughs. "But it’s full speed ahead now"

stories.title: Disruption to schools as teachers begin industrial action
stories.summary: Primary and secondary schools across the country are likely to experience disruptions from today as teachers begin industrial action. Members of the INTO and ASTI are commencing action in the form of a work-to-rule. In some schools, it will mean disruptions to early drop-offs and late collections outside of school hours. INTO members will no longer cooperate with Croke Park hours which will lead to the withdrawal of pre- and post-school supervision, meaning that pupils can only be on school premises during official school hours. Members will also refrain from attending staff meetings and formal parent-teacher meetings outside of school hours. A directive to ASTI members in secondary schools will see non-cooperation with Croke Park hours, non-cooperation with meetings held outside of normal school hours and non-cooperation with phone, email and other forms of electronic communication.

stories.title: Patients appeal for stem cell transplant lab at CUH
stories.summary: Patients with blood cancer such as leukemia are appealing to the HSE to reestablish a stem cell transplant laboratory at Cork University Hospital (CUH) to alleviate long hospital stays for them in Dublin and Galway, where stem cell labs are currently located. A lab at CUH was closed in the 2000s over compliance issues. It is estimated an investment of around €27 million would be required to restore stem cell treatment in Co Cork. Dan Sheehan is a dairy farmer from Blarney in Co Cork. In July of last year, he was diagnosed with acute leukemia. Mr Sheehan's treatment was a course of stem cell therapy, but that meant a six-week stay in St James's Hospital in Dublin, one of only two centres in the country providing stem cell transplantation. He is now campaigning for the development of a third laboratory to be located at CUH. Mr Sheehan cites the pressure on the existing unit at St James's Hospital and at University Hospital Galway, and the pressure extended stays at those hospitals put on patients from the south of the country and their families as the main reasons for supporting the re-instatement of the stem cell transplant unit at CUH.

stories.title: PTSB says remains 'fully focused' on BAWAG offer
stories.summary: PTSB said today that it had received no offer from Irish corporate finance firm Axis Capital, adding that a statement made by Axis on Friday was "highly speculative and conditional". Axis Capital said on Friday evening that it was considering making an offer for PTSB at a 7.7% premium to the proposed €1.6 billion sale to Austria's BAWAG Group supported by the Irish bank's shareholders. PTSB's board recommended BAWAG's offer in April and it was approved by shareholders in July, including by the Government which holds a 57.5% stake. The deal remains subject to regulatory and Irish High Court approvals. Axis said in a statement that shareholders would benefit from the opportunity to consider a competing proposal before the court meets later this month to approve the deal and that it was considering a possible cash offer of €3.20 per share compared to the €2.97 agreed with BAWAG. The Dublin-based firm said it would now engage with a number of potential funding and investment partners with a view to raising the necessary financing that would support the announcement of a firm intention to make an offer.

stories.title: Strait won't reopen until conditions met, warns Iran
stories.summary: The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until ⁠seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, state media reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf as saying. Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, with the US replying to this proposal last week via Qatari intermediaries. "The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met," Mr Qalibaf, who is Iran's top negotiator, was quoted as saying. He said Washington "must understand that the period of dragging out the (diplomatic) ‌process and dictating one-sided demands is over". A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had clarified its broad positions via mediators to the US response but that additional points remained to be communicated to Washington. "The Americans' propositions are more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue. We told them our focus in this stage is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz and the return to security in this waterway requires clear steps from the ‌US," spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.

stories.title: Power closes out with 67 as Smotherman prevails in Utah
stories.summary: Séamus Power finished tied for 21st as Austin Smotherman survived a back-nine double bogey to win his maiden PGA Tour title at the Bank of Utah Championship in Utah. Smotherman entered with a one-stroke lead over Doug Ghim and shot a three-under par 68 to finish on 26 under for the week, a new scoring record at the three-year-old tournament. He defeated Ghim by two shots after the latter posted a final-round 69 at Black Desert Resort. Power closed out his tournament with a blemish-free 67, with four birdies balanced out on the front and back nine. The Waterford native finished his tournament on 17-under par, nine shots adrift of Smotherman, who earns a two-year PGA Tour exemption and entry into the PGA Championship and The Players Championship. The 32-year-old is also projected to rise to No 51 in the FedEx Cup Fall points standings.

stories.title: Fitzmaurice tasked with banishing Galway's nearly man tag
stories.summary: Time will tell whether it's a perfect match but Éamonn Fitzmaurice's appointment as Galway senior manager heightens expectation as to what might unfold across the football scene in 2027. After neighbours Mayo emerged from the pack to end their famine last July, much of the commentariat honed in on the likelihood that Sam Maguire could reside in different homes over the next few years. Galway, naturally enough, will be hoping that a visit comes their way. It will soon be 26 years since the famous trophy wintered in Ireland's second largest county. During Pádraic Joyce's reign they became contenders again, reeled off four Connacht titles on the spin and contested two All-Ireland finals. The first of those saw them come up short against Kerry on a day David Clifford and Shane Walsh underlined their individual brilliance. Two years later and it was a case of one that got away. Admittedly not helped by Rob Finnerty going off early on, the Tribesmen, in a contest that at times skirted with turgidity, looked to have the measure of Armagh. But they lacked the ability to put a foot on the Orchard throat. Joyce's post-match reflections said it all: "It's a sickener, there's no doubt about that. I still have nightmares about it. I said to the boys afterwards, we'll regret it probably until we take our last breath in this world. But we had a great chance. We weren't clinical enough on the day, we didn't score enough. Simple as that." Shortcoming exposed. Sadly for Galway, such deficiencies were again to the fore during Joyce's final two years at the helm. An All-Ireland quarter-final against Meath looked to be swinging the Tribes' way going down the stretch, but the Royals had the greater energy when it mattered.

stories.title: Israel manager refuses to elaborate on racism claims
stories.summary: Israel manager Ran Ben Shimon insisted his "only focus" is related to matters on the pitch as his team prepares to take on the Republic of Ireland tomorrow in Serbia. Ireland's controversial Nations League fixtures against Israel – the 3-0 win in Debrecen and the 'home’ fixture in Backa Topola – have dominated the four-game international window, where the Boys in Green began with a 1-0 defeat in Kosovo and last time out secured a 2-2 draw with Austria. The build-up to the win over Israel was dominated by talks of a potential boycott, with goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrawing from the squad, saying he felt "it would be wrong to participate" in the fixture in light of the atrocities in the region. The negative undercurrent continued at the Irish press conference today when the media briefing ended abruptly after a disagreement between an Israeli journalist and FAI communications officer Kieran Crowley, with the journalist claiming that Irish players had called Israeli players "monkeys". Crowley responded by saying: "that's completely untrue" and declaring that the press conference was finished. That allegation follows on from an ongoing FAI investigation that striker Adam Idah was allegedly subjected to racist abuse from the sparsely populated stands in Debrecen.

stories.title: Leinster suffer second straight defeat against Sharks
stories.summary: Defending champions Leinster suffered a second successive defeat in the United Rugby Championship, falling to a 26-20 loss to the Sharks in Durban. The visitors struck first with a try for Robbie Henshaw in the 16th minute but Sharks pressure saw Manu Tshituka drive over to level the scores. Leinster found themselves camped on their line late in the half after Tom Clarkson was yellow-carded and a try from Lili Bester made it 14-7 at the break. The Irish side responded well at the start of the second half and Clarkson returned to the pitch to score their second try, while a penalty from Sam Prendergast briefly put them in front. But that prompted a flurry from the Sharks, with Andre Estherhuizen finishing off a swift counter-attack before an intercept try from Edwill van der Merwe. Leinster did at least finish with a bonus point after Andrew Osborne took Prendergast's kick in the corner and touched down.

stories.title: An unhappy medium: John O'Donnell's new Drama On One play
stories.summary: Fortune-tellers, mediums, psychics: do they really have a connection with the spirit world, or are they charlatans exploiting the vulnerabilities of others? I had been inclined to dismiss them as chancers. However, when I read Hilary Mantel's Beyond Black, a wickedly funny novel about a troubled psychic, I changed my mind. Maybe it’s not just their customers who feel depressed or unloved; maybe there’s no such thing as a happy medium. I started to explore the insecurities and desires of spiritualists and crystal-gazers. Some were – and are – tatty remnants of the vaudeville age, end-of-the-pier performers at the end of an era. But others do what they do not simply to make money, but to feel needed; to please. Where, I wondered, would a lonely clairvoyant go if she wanted to feel appreciated and loved? A bereavement therapy counselling session seemed the obvious place: and so, we first meet Fidelma, the main character in Horace, among her new 'friends' in the Grief Encounter group.. Horace is the teddy-bear Fidelma brings with her, a theatrical prop designed to endear her to strangers, to win hearts and unsuspecting minds. For a play about hearing voices, radio seems a particularly appropriate format; the perfect medium, you might say. Is Fidelma a misguided nuisance, or irredeemably evil? You’ll have to listen to the play and decide for yourself. But in earlier times a woman like Fidelma might have been condemned as a witch. The cartoon image of pointy hats and cats and spells may have evaporated, but in some places suspicions remain. The last prosecution in Britain under the 1735 Witchcraft Act was only eighty years ago. (Fidelma’s surname, Dunmore, is a nod to ‘The Dunmore Witch’, Alice Kyteler, the first woman charged with witchcraft in Ireland in 1324). Fidelma’s loneliness is at the dark heart of Horace, as is the sometimes desperate need of the bereaved to make contact with a lost loved one; though there are, I hope, moments of black humour also. And for a play about hearing voices, radio seems a particularly appropriate format; the perfect medium, you might say.

stories.title: First couple eliminated from Strictly Come Dancing
stories.summary: Celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton and his professional dance partner Amy Dowden have become the first couple eliminated from the new series of Strictly Come Dancing on BBC One. Their dances from the first two weeks of the show failed to impress the judges, who then sent them home. The pair left the competition following a Movie Week dance-off against actress Jaime Winstone and her professional dance partner, Carlos Gu. The judges' scores were added to those from the first live show, when there was no public vote. They were then combined with the results of Saturday night's public vote to decide the two lowest-scoring couples who would face the dance-off. Both couples performed their routines again, with Appleton and Dowden doing a Cha Cha to I'll Be Ready from Baywatch before Winstone and Gu did the same dance but to Oh, Pretty Woman from Pretty Woman.

stories.title: Review: I put two at-home exercise bikes to the test
stories.summary: Journalist Glenn Kelly was sent two smart bikes for the purpose of review. Here, he shares whether the tech-savvy equipment is worth the hefty price tag. With the evenings getting longer and the will to get outside for your daily workout slowly waning, now is the time to be looking at equipment that you can use indoors. As luck would have it, I might have just the machines for you. Home fitness is big business; in fact, according to Fortune Business Insights, it is worth $14 billion globally each year. That means manufacturers are stretching the boundaries of technology to replicate the feeling of outdoor activities from the comfort of your home. With that in mind, I was lucky enough to spend the last month testing two of the best premium exercise bikes on the market to see if they warrant your hard-earned money. NordicTrack and Echelon both compete in the premium studio bike tier through their flagship models, but which machine will win out when we test them on features, build quality and ride performance? Grab your water bottle and read on to find out.

stories.title: Childcare costs to be cut by at least €1,000 in Budget
stories.summary: The cost of full-time childcare for young children looks set to be cut by at least €1,000 annually per child in the Budget tomorrow. Discussions on the final Budget measures will continue throughout the day. The matter was discussed at length during the weekend, but the exact figures must be nailed down today. But it is clear at this point that for those in childcare for 45 hours a week, the changes will result in a cost cut for parents of at least €1,000 annually. This will be achieved through changes to the €96.30 weekly subsidy as well as lowering the current maximum €280 per week charge for childcare. The new rates are set to be introduced next September, and they will apply to children up to Senior Infants class.

stories.title: Breastfeeding rates rise to record high - HSE data
stories.summary: More than one in two three-month-old babies are being breastfeed, the highest rate since official records began in 1988, according to the HSE. HSE data suggests that 52% of three-month-old babies are breastfed while the percentage of babies breastfeed at birth increased to 66% last year. The number of babies being breastfed at three months has increased by 16% over the past decade, while the number being breastfed at birth increased by 2% from 2019 to 2025. Minister of State with special responsibility for Public Health Jennifer Murnane O'Connor said it is encouraging that figures continue to rise, noting investment in support and services. "Over the past year, we have listened to mothers and families about the experiences and factors that shape infant feeding decisions, while also consulting healthcare professionals and other stakeholders who support them. "This feedback will inform the new National Breastfeeding Strategy, which will be published later this year," she said.

stories.title: Does your employer actually know what you do at work?
stories.summary: Analysis: How the work we do is measured and turned into metrics an organisation can recognise is a perfect example of the Rumpelstiltskin economy Most of us are used to the idea that work has to be measured. We have targets and reviews, and we have to produce an account of what we have achieved. In my research on occupational wellbeing, what has really interested me is the point just before measurement, when work has to be turned into something that an organisation can recognise and sometimes reward. That conversion process can be almost invisible to the outsider, but it changes how people experience their job in many cases. What an organisation sees is often not the work itself, but something that stands in for it. This may be a score, a rating or the evidence attached to a review of your progress. In my research with academics, this meant that work had to be prepared for judgement. For example, good teaching was not necessarily visible to the institution simply because it had taken place. The relational and enjoyable work of supporting student learning had to be converted into something the organisation could more easily count, such as student satisfaction scores. I call this type of work the "labour of conversion". It matters not only because it takes time, but because the end measure can gradually become the version of the work that matters most to the organisation. I've come to think of this labour, and the constrained bargains it can involve, as the Rumpelstiltskin economy. You might recall the fairy tale from childhood. A boastful miller promises the king that his daughter can spin straw into gold, leaving her imprisoned in a tower to face an impossible task. In the midst of her anguish and distress, Rumpelstiltskin appears, offering to turn the straw into gold but for a price. At first, she offers him her necklace, then a ring. But as demand for gold continues, the price of the bargain also rises, until Rumpelstiltskin eventually asks for her firstborn child. She has little real choice, and she doesn’t know what the bargain will eventually cost her. But there is another part of the story that interests me. The king wants the gold, but has little interest in what it costs the miller’s daughter to produce it; he just wants the shiny product at the end. That constrained bargain may be familiar to anyone who has wondered whether their employer’s account of their performance matches their own. You know what a good day’s work looks like, but does the measure used by your organisation capture the same thing? If it doesn’t, you have a choice, but only to a point.

stories.title: Japan PM protests to US after marine accused of murder
stories.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has registered a protest with the United States after a US Marine was arrested on suspicion ⁠of robbing and murdering a Japanese woman in Okinawa. Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi in a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southernmost prefecture, yesterday and taking her wallet and backpack, police said. "The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and vicious incident is extremely regrettable," Ms Takaichi said in a statement. "The government of Japan strongly protests to the US side and strongly seeks maximum cooperation ‌with the investigation," as well ⁠as the tightening of discipline and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence, she said. Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, in comments carried by national broadcaster NHK, said: "Such an incident is unacceptable and I am deeply outraged." The US embassy and the Marine Corps expressed condolences over the incident and said they were cooperating ‌with the Japanese authorities.

stories.title: GAA round-up: All-Ireland champions fall
stories.summary: A number of county and provincial champions - as well as All-Ireland holders Daingean Uí Chúis - surrendered their titles as the club season continued to heat up around the country. All-Ireland winners Daingean uí Chúis saw their reign end as they exited the Kerry SFC, losing to Spa 1-17 to 1-11 in their Round 3 clash on Saturday. The Killarney side were full value for their win, with a late goal from Cian Murphy putting the gloss on things. Spa held a four-point advantage at the break - 0-12 to 1-05 - with Cathal Bambury netting for the now deposed champions. Daingean uí Chúis started the second half well and were only a point in arrears with over ten minutes left, thanks a Paul Geaney two-pointer, but they couldn't recover. Elsewhere, David Clifford stood out again as a late orange flag from him saw East Kerry edge Mid Kerry by the bare minimum - 1-12 to 1-11. Sunday's action saw An Ghaeltacht defeat Templenoe 1-14 to 0-15, while North Kerry were too strong for Na Gaeil on a 2-16 to 0-11.

stories.title: GPA seeks extra €700 a year per inter-county player
stories.summary: The Gaelic Players' Association (GPA) has asked Government for an extra €700 per player a year in support to help with what their CEO Tom Parsons described as "cost of living pressures". Inter-county players and representatives from the GPA met with Minister for Sport Patrick O'Donovan on Wednesday to seek the increase as part of the association's pre-budget engagement with Government. In total the GPA is seeking an additional €2.8m investment, which would bring support up from €1,800 to €2,500 per player. "Government funding is an important recognition of the extraordinary commitment made by inter-county players to our national games," said Parsons. "The findings presented to the Minister today give a clear picture of the reality behind that commitment. "At a time when the cost of living pressures are bearing down on players, Government has an opportunity to deliver something immediate and tangible for the current generation. We are asking for an additional €700 a year per player, bringing the support to €2,500.

stories.title: On love, loss and belonging in nature - Eoin Warner's new memoir
stories.summary:
In January 1979, when Eoin Warner was two years old, an oil tanker exploded in Bantry Bay. Among the fifty lives lost was Eoin's father. This devastating event cast a long shadow, shaping a childhood in which grief was a quiet presence at the table and in the empty front seat of the car. During this time, Eoin discovered how the natural world reflects so much of our human story, and it became his refuge. This memoir is not a straight line through loss; it's a series of vivid encounters with
the natural world, brimming with enchantment and wonder. In May 2010, a vixen appeared in Booterstown. What was fascinating about this visitor was that she would wander around in the revealing light of day, no doubt driven by a hungry litter of cubs. She would slip along the edge of the path in front of the houses and walk, Houdini-like, through the railings of our gate to visit our garden. We used to watch from the window, enthralled by this wild visitor as she sniffed the empty dog bowl and the hens, who were safe in their run. On one surreal occasion, the vixen even flirted with Mac. Although she was smaller than him, he was delighted by the female attention. They played for ages, running rings around each other on the small lawn. Mac had a bit of a roving eye. A relaxed human leg or a vixen were all fair game in his mind. Adaptation to environmental change is a natural part of evolution, a process that unfolds over generations in which the strongest survive. Unfortunately, in this epoch of human-induced environmental change, the pace is so rapid that many species cannot adapt quickly enough to survive. Some species, however, are adjusting and leveraging the skills they already possess to adapt to this rapidly changing landscape. The red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is one. Their natural range spans extreme climates across the whole northern hemisphere, where they have made almost every habitat their home. Historically, the shy fox has preferred to avoid human contact and has made its home in rural settings. However, as we encroach on the foxes' habitat with our growing towns and cities, making their habitat ours, they adapt, moving into our urban areas. Take a night-time drive at any time of year through the lamp-lit streets of Dublin and you are almost guaranteed to see a fox moving in the shadows. On a warm June evening, the front door was open and the vixen walked into the house, meeting me in the living room. We both stopped dead in our tracks, six feet apart, and stared at each other. I was startled, as I’m sure she was, but if so, she certainly did not show it. She stared at me with emotionless amber eyes, her gaze examining me. Her sharply cocked ears were faced squarely in my direction and didn’t move. She looked incongruous among the brightly coloured blue and yellow toys. Once she grew bored of our staring contest, she turned and left without even a courtesy glance back. It was the strangest feeling, as if this were an affront. The fox has taught me to honour these shared spaces, so that I now acknowledge I am entering another's space – the more-than-human world. Now, whenever I enter a woodland, a bog or the sea, I pause and remind myself that I am the visitor.

stories.title: Kilkenny bakery makes history at Blas na hÉireann food awards
stories.summary: Arán Bakery & Bistro has been named Supreme Champion at the Blas na hÉireann Irish Food Awards for the second time, making history as the first producer to ever take home the coveted title more than once. The announcement was made at an awards ceremony this evening, as part of a four-day celebration, taking place from 1 to 4 October in Daingean Uí Chúis, Co. Kerry. Now in their 19th year, the Blas na hÉireann awards are famed for celebrating produce from across the country. This year, over 3,000 products from every county in Ireland competed across more than 200 categories. The most notable awards, though, are undoubtedly Supreme Champion, sponsored by Bord Bia, and Best Artisan Producer, sponsored by LEO Network. Arán Bakery & Bistro were crowned Supreme Champion thanks to their "exceptional breads and pastries", which have "consistently impressed" the Blas na hÉireann judges. Having previously been a finalist, gold medal winner and Supreme Champion in 2022, Arán has returned to the top spot four years later with its Arán spelt sourdough – making Bart Pawlukojc and his team the first ever recipients to win the Supreme Champion title twice.
